chapter_theme: Songs at Kazhugumalai (கழுகுமலை): the poet confesses the bitter infatuation with women who sell their breasts and seize men's wealth, refuses any longer to plead his poverty before base men, and asks to swim the wave of births to the pure feet; the praise names Rama, Murugan's vel given by Siva, and Murugan become a vengai tree for Valli.

632.reading: The poet says that the infatuation with women of lisping speech who take wealth and sell their breasts has been bitter beyond bitter, and that he, bewildered as a child, can no longer, in his youth, plead his poverty before many base and cruel men. The praise names the cloud-dark nephew of Vishnu who threw the vel so that Sura, who opposed Rama's bow, fell, and Murugan at the great town of Kazhugumalai, rich in virtue, among plantain and areca and fields where bees hum.
632.nuance: The two humiliations are set side by side: money lost to women (நிதிக் கொள்வார், முலையை விலை செய்வார்) and then poverty pleaded to the wicked (பதகர் ... இடத்திலே மிக வறுமை புகல்வதே). இனி முடியாதே, 'no longer can I', is the plea. The praise line on Sura and the bow is hard to construe.

633.reading: The poet describes whores who hide and bare their breasts, loosen their clothes and lie down, kiss again and again on beds of flowers, embrace until a man is shaken, destroy men's strength of mind and snatch their wealth from their hands while their passion is great, and asks whether a relationship with them can be right. The praise names Rama who bent the bow so that Ravana's ten crowns flew and his body was pierced, Murugan nephew of that archer, the victorious vel given by Siva who bears the moon and Ganga, at Kazhugumalai.
633.nuance: வேசைகள் is the bluntest name; the sequence runs from seduction (முத்திக் கொடுப்பர்) to the destruction of the man's will (மனவலியைத் தட்டழிப்பர்) to the theft (பொருளைக் கைப் பறிப்பர்). மால் பெரிது: they take it while the man's infatuation is at its height.

634.reading: The poet, a servant with an unending longing for women whose eyes are bent arrows and whose lovemaking is sweet as nectar, sleepless day and night, asks whether he will swim the long wave of birth and reach the pure feet. The praise names Murugan's vel against Sura hiding in the sea of ships and sharks, Brahma afraid, the lone vel-bearer riding the peacock on the heron hill, the Kumara who took the form of a vengai tree to the hunters' grief so that the girl melted, and the Lord who gives devotees and poets the rare thing they ask, as much as they ask.
634.nuance: பிறவி அலையை நீந்தி அமல அடி வந்து அடைவேனோ recalls the Kural's sea of births crossed by the feet. வேங்கை வடிவு மருவும் குமரேசா: in the Valli story Murugan hid as a vengai tree when her kin came; the text names it. குருகு மலை, heron hill, stands for the shrine's own name, the vulture hill.

links.note: Both describe women who take the wealth from a man's hand once he is caught; the Naladiyar adds that he is laughed at, 633 that his very strength of mind is destroyed.
Both confess the humiliation of pleading before patrons; 15 tells the flattery, 632 says he can no longer bear to plead his poverty to base and cruel men after women took his wealth.
The Kural says only those who join the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; 634 asks in the same image whether he will swim the long wave of birth and reach the pure feet.
